messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus is a twenty-eight-year-old financial analyst, married and living in a suburban home with his wife and their three-year-old daughter. Eight months ago, his daughter was hospitalized with a severe bacterial infection that spiraled into sepsis. For three days the doctors could not guarantee she would survive. Marcus sat in a sterile hospital room, watching her tiny body fight, listening to the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator, and memorizing the flat gray light coming through the window. She recovered fully, but the experience carved a wound that has not healed.

Now, any reminder of that time can send him into a panicked state. On a mild, overcast morning, when the light through his office window matches that hospital gray, Marcus finds his chest tightening and his breath shortening. He has come to believe that such weather is a sign that something terrible is about to happen again. A news segment about childhood illness, even a brief mention on the radio during his commute, makes him grip the steering wheel until his knuckles whiten. He reacts as if he is in immediate danger even though nothing is wrong. He has started scanning every room he enters for exits—at work he chooses the desk closest to the stairwell, and at restaurants he sits facing the door, cataloging alternate routes in case he needs to flee. At night, he lies awake for hours, his senses trained on every sound from his daughter’s room, too alert to let sleep come.

These triggers also feed a corrosive self-appraisal. When Marcus hears about another sick child, or sees a toddler in the grocery store, the thought surfaces: *I should have protected her and I failed.* He did not fail—the medical team acted swiftly—but the feeling is visceral. He feels like a stranger to himself. The person he is now, always bracing for catastrophe, is unrecognizable compared to the easygoing father he used to be. He does not know who he is anymore. The more these negative appraisals take hold, the more acutely he notices triggers. He becomes hyperattentive to any cough or sniffle from his daughter, and to worried glances from his wife, interpreting them as confirmations that danger is present.

His memory of the hospitalization is both vivid and fragmentary. He can replay the exact image of the heart monitor’s numbers dropping, the doctor’s face, the rain streaming down the hospital window—but just as the memory threatens to reach the worst moment, he pushes it away before it completes. He has come to believe that if he lets himself fully remember, he will break. Yet the images intrude unbidden, mostly visual snapshots that flash into his mind when he is trying to work on spreadsheets. Each intrusion reinforces his belief that he failed to protect his daughter. In turn, the constant sense of threat keeps the memory alive: whenever he feels that sudden alarm, the hospital scenes return with renewed intensity. And because he is always on edge, he spots triggers where they might not exist—a child crying in the grocery store, a siren outside—and the cycle tightens.

Avoidance has come to dominate his life. He no longer watches the news, changed his commute to avoid passing the hospital, and has asked his wife to take their daughter to the park without him. At work, his concentration has slipped; a colleague noticed his jumpiness and asked if he was okay. Marcus brushed it off, but the question stung. He feels trapped in a version of himself he does not respect.

What finally brought him to seek help was a minor incident: his daughter developed a mild fever, and within seconds he was kneeling beside her bed, trembling, trying to remember the breathing exercises the nurses had taught him. His wife found him there and gently told him that their daughter was fine, that the fever would pass. Marcus knew she was right, but he could not make his body believe it. He is terrified that he will pass this vigilance on to his daughter, but he also cannot imagine living any other way. He hopes therapy can give him back the person he used to be—the father who could laugh on a rainy day instead of bracing for the worst.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals cause or lead to memory recall; instead, memory intrudes spontaneously and then triggers negative appraisals.
The vignette does not show that memory causes the patient to notice triggers; instead, threat leads to hypervigilance for triggers.
